headline: High: Goose can write and modify shared files while Pathway is read-only, creating prompt-injection and cascading-error risk; compliance risk is low because Pathway touches no data by profile.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Goose can read/write the user filesystem and use MCP, and its state is shared via filesystem; Pathway has no file I/O, so the main bridge is Goose ingesting attacker-controlled files or outputs from a shared workspace. That makes injection plausible in default coding workflows, though not proven for Pathway itself.
conditions: IF Goose reads content from a shared workspace that Pathway can also influence
IF an MCP server or file bridge passes Pathway output into Goose prompts without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable shared-workspace handoff for prompt-bearing files
Add provenance tags to any Pathway-produced text before Goose reads it
Restrict Goose MCP servers to allowlisted, read-only endpoints
Review and sanitize files before Goose ingests them

B_data_leakage.rationale: Goose can touch source code and files in cwd and may send context to configured model providers, while Pathway is documented as not reading files or using network egress. The pair does not show a direct shared data sink, so leakage is limited to Goose’s own handling of local files rather than a two-way exfiltration path.
conditions: IF Goose is pointed at sensitive files in the shared cwd
IF configured model providers receive those files in Goose context
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of Goose’s working directory
Use a redacted staging directory for Goose inputs
Disable or narrow Goose access to secrets-bearing paths
Confirm Pathway remains offline and fileless in the deployment

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Goose has filesystem write and git modification, while Pathway has no write, shell, or git capabilities. There is no overlapping mutable resource in the profiles, so direct capability conflict is weak; the only plausible conflict is Goose contending with external files Pathway may reference, which is not a shared write surface here.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same git working tree through an external orchestrator
IF Pathway is wrapped by another component that adds write access not shown in its profile
mitigations: Assign Goose and Pathway separate directories
Serialize any git writes through one operator
Lock the repo before Goose edits files
Verify Pathway is not wrapped with hidden write permissions

D_cascading_error.rationale: Goose can generate code and file changes, and Pathway can consume pipeline-style data, so a bad Goose output could be treated as input to downstream processing. Pathway is not documented as verifying Goose’s outputs, so the pair has a plausible default cascade from generated content into later actions, though Pathway itself is not an action-taking agent.
conditions: IF Pathway ingests Goose-produced files or records without validation
IF Goose-generated artifacts are used as authoritative inputs to a pipeline
mitigations: Insert schema validation between Goose and Pathway
Require human review of Goose outputs before ingestion
Add checksum or signature checks on Goose-generated artifacts
Reject malformed or unverified records at the Pathway boundary

E_compliance.rationale: Goose handles model-provider keys and extension tokens and can touch local files, while Pathway’s profile shows no data classes, no file access, and no network egress. There is no documented residency or retention mismatch between them, so compliance risk is limited to Goose’s own handling of local secrets rather than a pairwise policy conflict.
conditions: IF Goose is used on regulated data stored in the cwd
IF Goose forwards those files to external model providers under a policy that forbids it
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Goose sessions
Use a local-only provider configuration where possible
Rotate any exposed extension tokens after testing
Document retention and residency rules for Goose inputs
